summary: This experimental memo adds digital signature authentication to OSPF link-state data and a certification mechanism for router data. It covers extra LSA processing, key management, and migration from or coexistence with standard OSPF version 2.

plainLanguage.summary: Each router signs its messages, so others can tell they are real and not forged.

questions: what is a router public key lsa
how does secure ospf authenticate lsas
what is a trusted entity in ospf
subtitle: An experimental design that has every OSPF router sign its link-state data so others can verify who sent it.

tldr.problem: OSPF's simple password is sent in the clear and keyed MD5 only protects packets between neighbors, so routing data flooded through faulty or subverted routers is not authenticated end to end.
tldr.mechanism: Each router signs its own LSAs with a private key, publishes its public key in a new Public Key LSA certified by a Trusted Entity, and receivers check the signatures and the address ranges the router may advertise.
tldr.outcome: LSAs gain end-to-end integrity and authentication, but ABRs, ASBRs and a router's own claims remain vulnerable. It is an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2154 is an Experimental memo from June 1997, not an Internet standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoletes or updates it, and the text defines only one signature algorithm, RSA-MD5.

sections.title: Authenticating Routing Data
sections.content:
OSPF offers a "simple password" that travels in the clear, so any listener can discover and reuse it. Keyed MD5 between neighbors protects the packets passed between them, but it does not authenticate routing data flooded from its source to its eventual destination through routers that may be faulty or subverted.

This memo adds digital signatures to link state advertisements (LSAs). The neighbor-to-neighbor algorithm still protects Hello, Link State Request, Link State Update and Database Description packets, while each flooded LSA is individually signed by its originator. The signature stays with the data, giving end-to-end integrity and authentication, and if a faulty router originates bad data, the signature identifies the source.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing notes down a row of kids is risky because someone might change a note. If the writer signs it, everyone can tell if it was changed or who wrote it.

sections.title: Keys, Certificates and Trusted Entities
sections.content:
Each router holds a private key and a public key. It runs a one-way hash (such as MD5 or SHA) over an LSA, signs the digest with the private key, and appends the signature. Any other router can verify it with the public key.

Public keys travel in a new Router Public Key LSA (PKLSA), flooded like any other LSA. Since anyone can claim to be a router, a Trusted Entity (TE) issues a certificate that binds the router's identity to its key. The certificate holds the router id, role, permitted address ranges, a timestamp and the public key, and is signed by the TE. The RFC does not say how a TE must be built or reached. It requires that a TE has a unique TE Id, gives each router key a unique Rtr Key Id, and timestamps certificates consistently. Routers need not have synchronized clocks, but TEs do.

Every router is configured with its own certificate and with the TE public keys it needs to verify other routers' certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted office hands out ID cards. A router shows its card, other routers check the office's stamp, and then they trust the router's signature.

sections.title: Signed LSAs and PKLSA Processing
sections.content:
A signed LSA is a normal LSA with key identification, a signature and a signature length appended. The top bit of the LS type field marks the presence of a signature. A verified LSA is stored for routing. A failed one must be discarded. If the key has not yet arrived, the LSA is held for the configurable MAX_TRANSIT_DELAY and discarded if the key does not show up in that time. For Router Links LSAs, each network link must fall in an address range certified for that router, otherwise the LSA is logged and discarded.

A PKLSA is verified in two ways: the router's own signature, and the TE certification inside it. Only one PKLSA is kept per router, and the one with the most recent Create Time wins. PKLSAs are sent before other LSAs when databases are synchronized, and are flooded only within an area, except that an ASBR's PKLSAs go wherever AS external LSAs go.

The age field is normally unsigned because other routers must update it. To stop a faulty router from aging out others' LSAs, the signature covers the age field only when the originator creates the LSA with age MaxAge. Thus only the originator can flush an LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: A router only believes a message if the signature checks out and the message talks only about places that router is allowed to talk about.

sections.title: Replacing Router and TE Keys
sections.content:
Router keys should be changed periodically, and at once if one is compromised. A router may have one valid key per area at a time, so a newer key revokes the older one without a revocation list: the certificate's Create Time shows which is more recent. To change a key, the router obtains a new certificate, floods a new PKLSA, and re-signs and sends all its own LSAs. Receivers age LSAs signed with the old key to MaxAge - MAX_TRANSIT_DELAY.

TE key replacement is harder, because all certificates depending on the old key must be reissued and every router needs the new key. The RFC describes the method its implementation tested: set a distribution interval (TE_KEY_DIST_INT) long enough to install the new key everywhere, then have each router start using it when its timer fires. A router that misses the key logs errors and routes on its old database until those LSAs time out. The simple fix is to load the key and restart.

Multiple signature algorithms, multiple TEs and multiple keys per router are permitted. Each has a scope, and routers that cannot verify an LSA discard it and do not flood it.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a lock is easy for one door. Changing the master lock for the whole building needs everyone to get the new key first.

sections.title: Mixing Signed and Unsigned Areas
sections.content:
An autonomous system can contain "signed" and "unsigned" areas, but never both kinds of LSA in one area. Each area has an environment flag (signed is 1, unsigned is 0). An ABR between a signed and unsigned area must handle both kinds, generate signed summaries for one side and unsigned for the other, and must not flood signed LSAs into unsigned areas or the reverse.

This keeps routing available across the whole AS, but authentication holds only for routes inside, or crossing only, signed areas. AS external routes are harder, and to reach them from every area the RFC suggests placing the ASBR on the backbone and advertising default routes to the backbone.

A router that is both ABR and ASBR must use the same key, signature algorithm, certifying TE and signed/unsigned setting for all attached areas. Otherwise multiple versions of its AS external LSAs and PKLSAs would be flooded.
sections.plainLanguage: Some neighborhoods use signed letters and some do not. The post office at the border never mixes the two kinds in one neighborhood.

sections.title: Remaining Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
A router can still distribute wrong data about things it is responsible for. ABRs can inject incorrect Summary LSAs. The RFC sketches ways ABRs could corroborate each other, but did not add them because they cost much extra processing and messaging, and the vulnerability is isolated to a few points in each area.

An internal router can announce a wrong metric, or a nonexistent stub network or host route. The Dijkstra check can catch a fake link to a transit network only when the other end disagrees. The damage is limited to its certified address ranges, and the signatures identify the culprit. ASBRs stay an unprotected vulnerability because nothing in the AS can authorize the external networks they announce, so the RFC says they need protecting by other means.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing proves who said something, not that it is true. A router can still tell fibs about its own streets.
